interview_metadata.name: John Papagno
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Columbus, Ohio, in a pretty middle-class Italian-American family. My childhood was very much pasta on Sundays, cousins everywhere at the Columbus Italian Festival, Buckeye football on TV, and my parents pushing school without making it feel like some elite pressure cooker. I was a curious kid, the kind who would take apart a radio and then get in trouble because I could not put it back together, but I also liked drawing and music, so I was never purely a math-and-science guy. I went to Ohio State and got a bachelor's degree in management information systems, with enough marketing and communications classes that I started seeing business as storytelling plus data. After college I got into tech sales almost by accident through an internship connection, and I found out I was good at translating technical stuff into language clients could actually care about. Relationship-wise, I have dated seriously a couple of times, but I have never been married and I do not have kids. My thirties have been about building a career as a sales manager, keeping close to my family here in Columbus, and trying not to let work swallow the creative parts of me. I play pickup basketball, hike on weekends, cook Italian food when I have time, go to contemporary art shows, and I try to keep my emotions from running the whole show by meditating and journaling.

follow_ups.question: When you think of your childhood home, what specific routines or memories come back first?
follow_ups.response: Sunday dinner is the first thing. My mom would start sauce in the morning, my dad would be half-watching a Browns or Buckeyes game, and my sister and I would be setting the table while relatives drifted in.

follow_ups.question: Was there someone early on who shaped your interest in both technical work and creative work?
follow_ups.response: My mom was the creative one because she loved museums and music, and my dad was the practical systems guy. I think I absorbed both: make it work, but make it mean something.

follow_ups.question: How often do you still see family now that you are an adult?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a week or every other week. I will go to my parents' place for dinner, or we will meet at a restaurant, and holidays are still very family-centered.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was probably around my junior year at Ohio State. I had started out thinking I would do something more technical, maybe systems analysis or product work, because I liked structure and problem-solving. Then I had a summer internship where I sat in on client demos, and I watched one sales engineer completely change the mood in a room by taking a dry software feature and turning it into a story about a manager getting home to their kids earlier. That hit me hard. I realized I did not just want to build or configure systems; I wanted to be the person connecting the system to human stakes. My parents were a little nervous because sales sounded unstable compared with a straightforward tech job, but I took an entry-level sales development role after graduation. It was humbling, lots of rejection and call blocks and learning Salesforce from the ground up, but it shaped me. That choice put me on the path to managing a team and thinking long-term about leadership and maybe eventually consulting.

follow_ups.question: What did your parents say when you chose sales instead of a more traditional technical role?
follow_ups.response: My dad asked about salary and benefits immediately, which is very him. My mom was more like, if this is where your energy is, try it, but do not become someone you do not like.

follow_ups.question: Do you remember the first job title you had after graduation?
follow_ups.response: Sales development representative. It was mostly prospecting, qualifying leads, logging everything in Salesforce, and trying not to sound terrified on the phone.

follow_ups.question: What made you stick with it through the rejection?
follow_ups.response: I liked the scoreboard aspect, honestly. If I changed my script or my research process, I could see the numbers move, and that made the rejection feel like data instead of just personal failure.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice, but it was not perfectly planned. I remember making a spreadsheet comparing technical analyst roles with sales roles, and then still choosing the sales path because I felt more alive in those conversations.

follow_ups.question: What was on that spreadsheet?
follow_ups.response: Starting pay, likely career path, stability, what skills I would build, and honestly a gut-feeling column because I knew numbers alone were not telling the whole story.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk it through with anyone besides your parents?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a professor and a friend from my business classes. The professor told me that being technical and persuasive was a rare combination, and that stuck with me.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. I could have used more formal mentorship about what tech sales actually looked like as a career, not just a job people fall into. Ohio State had resources, but I did not know how to navigate them well then.

follow_ups.question: What kind of mentoring would have helped most?
follow_ups.response: Shadowing people in different roles for a day would have been huge. I wanted to see the calendar, the pressure, the compensation structure, the boring parts too.

follow_ups.question: Do you mentor younger people now because of that?
follow_ups.response: A little. I talk with new reps and occasionally meet students through alumni events, especially people who are technical but not sure they want to code all day.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner right now, and I do not have children. The core people for me are my parents, Anthony and Maria, who still live in the Columbus area, and my younger sister, Gina, who is married and lives in Westerville. My parents are retired or semi-retired now, and they are the kind of people who still ask if I am eating enough even though I am 36. Gina and I are close, though we communicate more through texts, memes, and practical favors than deep dramatic phone calls. She has one little boy, my nephew Luca, and being an uncle has been a really good part of my life. I am at my parents' table pretty often, especially for birthdays, holidays, and random Sundays when my mom decides everyone needs lasagna. I also feel some responsibility as the local son, like helping with tech stuff, driving them to appointments if needed, and being available. It is a warm family, but also loud and opinionated, so I have learned to take a walk when the volume gets too high.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your nephew?
follow_ups.response: Maybe twice a month on average, more around holidays. I try to be the uncle who shows up with a book, a soccer ball, or some ridiculous science kit.

follow_ups.question: What kinds of practical things do you help your parents with?
follow_ups.response: Phones, streaming apps, medical portal passwords, that whole universe. I also help my dad compare insurance paperwork because he hates dealing with websites.

follow_ups.question: Are you dating currently?
follow_ups.response: A little, but not seriously. I use apps on and off, and I have met people through friends, but right now work and my own routines take up a lot of space.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My sister's husband, Mark, is part of the immediate orbit, and we get along well. I also have a couple of aunts, uncles, and cousins in Columbus who feel close because Italian families do not always draw clean lines between immediate and extended family.

follow_ups.question: Do you see the extended family regularly?
follow_ups.response: Mostly for holidays, graduations, the Italian Festival, and big Sunday meals. It is not weekly, but it is steady.

follow_ups.question: Who in the family are you most likely to call for advice?
follow_ups.response: Usually Gina if it is personal, my dad if it is practical money or house stuff, and my mom if I need someone to calm me down.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yes, I have a pretty active friend circle, though it is scattered across different parts of my life. My closest friend is probably Marcus, who I met playing pickup basketball, and we usually play or grab coffee once a week. I have a couple of college friends, Evan and Priya, who are still in Columbus, and we do dinner or trivia every month or so. I am also close with a coworker named Leah because we have been through some intense quarter-end pushes together. Then there are lighter but important communities: the Columbus Hoops Collective, my hiking group, and people from improv class. I like having different circles because each one pulls out a different version of me.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Marcus usually do together besides basketball?
follow_ups.response: We will hit a diner after Sunday runs, watch Cavs games, or talk through work stress in a very unpolished but helpful way.

follow_ups.question: How often do you go to improv classes or workshops?
follow_ups.response: Usually one evening a week when I am in a session. If work gets crazy I skip a term, but I keep coming back because it gets me out of my head.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in the Clintonville/Old North area of Columbus, in the 43202 zip code. It is a good fit for me because it is walkable by Columbus standards, close to coffee shops, casual restaurants, the library, and not too far from Ohio State. My apartment is in an older brick building with creaky floors and a lot more character than storage space. I like that I can walk to get coffee on Saturday morning and still get downtown or to the Short North pretty quickly for a gallery opening or dinner. There are students nearby, young professionals, older homeowners, and families, so it has a mixed feel. It is not fancy in a polished way, but it feels lived-in and familiar.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often in the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: A coffee shop near High Street, the library branch, and Whetstone Park when I want to clear my head. I also have a go-to pizza place for lazy Friday nights.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A little. We say hi in the hallway and text about packages or parking, but it is not a building where everyone hangs out together.

follow_ups.question: How long have you lived there?
follow_ups.response: About four years. I moved there when I wanted to be closer to the parts of the city where I actually spend time.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel pretty safe overall. There are occasional car break-ins and porch package thefts, so I am careful, but I do not feel unsafe walking around during the day or early evening.

follow_ups.question: Do you change your behavior at night?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I pay more attention if I am walking late, and I usually take main streets instead of cutting through darker side streets.

follow_ups.question: Have you personally had anything stolen there?
follow_ups.response: One package disappeared a couple of years ago. It was annoying, not traumatic, and now I use pickup lockers for expensive stuff.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is convenience and a sense of neighborhood texture: coffee, parks, old houses, people walking dogs, that kind of thing. The downside is parking, rent creeping up, and noise from students or traffic on weekends.

follow_ups.question: What would make you move?
follow_ups.response: If rent jumped too much or if I decided to buy a place. I like the area, but I am not emotionally attached to this specific apartment.

follow_ups.question: Do you imagine staying in Columbus long-term?
follow_ups.response: Probably, unless a major career opportunity pulled me somewhere else. My family, network, and routines are here.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live alone. It is a one-bedroom apartment, and there is nobody else staying with me right now. I like living alone because my workdays involve so much talking and managing other people's energy that I need quiet at home. My place is not minimalist, exactly; there are books, a couple of framed prints, kitchen equipment, and a small desk where I tinker with Arduino projects. I do host friends occasionally for dinner or a Cavs game, but it is not a roommate situation.

follow_ups.question: Do you have pets?
follow_ups.response: No. I like dogs, but with travel and long workdays I do not think it would be fair right now.

follow_ups.question: What room do you spend the most time in?
follow_ups.response: The kitchen and living room area. I cook, work on my laptop at the table sometimes, and decompress there after work.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. It is just me as the permanent household.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone stayed with you recently?
follow_ups.response: Not recently. A friend crashed on my couch one night after a late Cavs game, but that is occasional.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect that to change soon?
follow_ups.response: No, I expect to keep living alone for now.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Friends or family might stay one night once in a while, but nobody stays here regularly.

follow_ups.question: Who is most likely to stay over?
follow_ups.response: Probably an out-of-town college friend visiting Columbus.

follow_ups.question: Do you host family overnight?
follow_ups.response: Rarely, because most of my family is local.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, there is no one who usually lives here and is away.

follow_ups.question: So your household count is one?
follow_ups.response: Yes, one person.

follow_ups.question: Any shared custody or regular child stays?
follow_ups.response: No, I do not have children.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday are pretty structured around work. I usually wake up around 6:30, meditate for ten minutes if I am being disciplined, make coffee, check my calendar, and either drive to the office or work from home. Mondays are pipeline review and forecast days, Tuesdays and Wednesdays are heavier client calls and one-on-ones with reps, Thursdays are usually deal strategy, and Fridays I try to clean up admin before the weekend. After work I rotate between pickup basketball, the gym, improv class, cooking at home, or just crashing with a show. Saturdays are errands, museum visits, hiking when the weather is decent, or seeing friends. Sundays are basketball in the morning sometimes and family dinner if my parents are hosting.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually stop working?
follow_ups.response: On a normal day around 6:00 or 6:30, but quarter-end can push that to 8:00 or later.

follow_ups.question: Which day feels most packed?
follow_ups.response: Tuesday. That is when client meetings, rep coaching, and internal strategy calls tend to stack up.

follow_ups.question: What is the one routine you try hardest to protect?
follow_ups.response: Sunday morning basketball or a walk. If I lose that, the whole week feels more reactive.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a sales manager for a B2B technology company based in Columbus. We sell software and data tools to mid-market companies, so my work is a mix of coaching account executives, inspecting pipeline, joining bigger client presentations, forecasting revenue, and translating product capabilities into business outcomes. My official hours are roughly 8:30 to 5:30, Monday through Friday, but sales does not fit perfectly inside that box. If a client on the West Coast wants a late call or a proposal is due, I work later. I am hybrid, usually in the office two or three days a week and home the rest. I do not have a second paid job.

follow_ups.question: What tools do you use most during the day?
follow_ups.response: Salesforce constantly, plus Slack, Zoom, Google Sheets, Gong, and whatever deck we are building for a client.

follow_ups.question: How many people do you manage?
follow_ups.response: Seven account executives directly, plus I work closely with two sales development reps and a solutions engineer.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I have a few. I help my parents with tech and paperwork when they need it, and I try to check in with my sister once a week. I meal prep loosely on Sundays, not like a fitness influencer, more like making sauce or roasting vegetables so I do not order takeout three nights in a row. I journal a few nights a week, especially when I am wound up from work. I also track workouts and spending in apps because if I do not measure things, I drift. The trick is not letting tracking become its own weird form of procrastination.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually meal prep?
follow_ups.response: Chicken, vegetables, farro or pasta, sometimes a big pot of sauce. If I am ambitious, I make gnocchi and freeze some.

follow_ups.question: What do you journal about?
follow_ups.response: Mostly what set me off emotionally, what I could have handled better, and one or two things I am grateful for so it is not just a complaint log.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is that I have been more intentional about mornings. Last year I got into a bad pattern of waking up and immediately checking Slack, which meant I started the day already irritated or anxious. Around the beginning of this year, I started putting my phone across the room and doing coffee, meditation, and a short workout before opening work apps. I have also been going into the office slightly more because newer reps need in-person coaching. Socially, I have been saying yes to more hiking and improv again after a stretch where I let work dominate.

follow_ups.question: What helped you make the morning change stick?
follow_ups.response: I made it physical: phone charger across the room, work apps muted until 8:00, workout clothes set out. If it depends on willpower, I lose.

follow_ups.question: Have you noticed a difference?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I am still reactive, but I catch myself faster, and I do not walk into the first meeting already carrying ten invisible arguments.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so I do not have a school-year routine like that. The closest child-related routine in my life is occasionally helping my sister with my nephew if she and her husband need backup, but that is not a regular childcare schedule.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever pick up or babysit your nephew?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally on a weekend afternoon or evening, but not on school days as a standing thing.

follow_ups.question: Would children be part of your future hopes?
follow_ups.response: Possibly, but I am not treating it like a guaranteed milestone. It would depend on the relationship and whether I could be present enough.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences with law enforcement have been limited and mostly routine. I have had a couple of traffic stops, one for speeding on I-71 and one for a taillight, and both were tense in the way traffic stops are tense, but nothing escalated. I have called the non-emergency line once about a car break-in near my building. I am aware that my experience as a white guy in Columbus is not the same as what some friends describe. That awareness became much sharper after 2020, because I heard stories from people I know that were very different from mine.

follow_ups.question: How did you feel during those traffic stops?
follow_ups.response: Nervous and annoyed, but I also expected I would be treated basically fairly. That expectation itself is something I have thought about.

follow_ups.question: What happened with the car break-in report?
follow_ups.response: An officer took a report, but nothing came of it. It was mostly for insurance and documentation.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: During the 2020 protests in Columbus, I remember seeing a much heavier police presence downtown than I was used to. I was not in the middle of any confrontation, but the atmosphere stuck with me.

follow_ups.question: Were you downtown during any protest?
follow_ups.response: I attended one peaceful march during the day. I left before evening because I did not want to be in a volatile situation.

follow_ups.question: Did that change your view of policing?
follow_ups.response: It made me think more about accountability and crowd control, yes. I do not think of policing as one simple category anymore.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and no one in my immediate family has either. A college friend had a DUI in his twenties, and I remember how much shame and disruption it caused him.

follow_ups.question: Were you close to him at the time?
follow_ups.response: Yes, close enough that I picked him up once after court. It was one of those moments where everyone realized we were not invincible kids anymore.

follow_ups.question: Did it change your own behavior?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. I am careful about rideshares now if I have more than a drink or two.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote pretty consistently. I have missed a small local election here or there, but I vote in presidential, midterm, and most city elections. I usually vote early in person or by mail because my work calendar can get unpredictable. Local races matter to me more than they used to, especially city council, school levies, judges, and transit-related issues. I do not go door-knocking every weekend or anything, but I try to be an informed voter.

follow_ups.question: Where do you get information before voting?
follow_ups.response: The League of Women Voters guide, local news, candidate websites, and sometimes conversations with friends who follow local politics more closely.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but carefully. My family is mixed enough politically that I try not to turn Sunday dinner into cable news.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as center-left or pragmatic progressive. I usually vote Democratic, and I care about health care access, climate policy, public education, reproductive rights, and basic protections for workers. At the same time, I work in business and sales, so I do not think markets or companies are automatically bad. I just think incentives need guardrails because I have seen how numbers can make people behave in ways they would not defend morally if they slowed down. I am pro-immigration in a practical and human sense, probably influenced by family stories of Italian relatives and by working with people from different backgrounds. On policing and race, I support accountability and reform, though I try to keep learning because I know I did not grow up having to think about those systems the same way others did. I am not a revolutionary person politically; I like competent institutions, good data, and leaders who can actually execute. What frustrates me most is performative outrage that turns every issue into a brand identity.

follow_ups.question: What issues would most strongly influence your vote?
follow_ups.response: Health care, democracy and voting rights, climate, and whether the person seems competent rather than just loud.

follow_ups.question: Are there any conservative ideas you agree with?
follow_ups.response: I respect fiscal discipline when it is real and not just used to cut programs people dislike. I also think local communities should have room to solve problems in ways that fit them.

follow_ups.question: Do you donate to campaigns?
follow_ups.response: Small amounts occasionally, usually to a candidate or local issue campaign, not large recurring donations.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become less tolerant of political theater and more focused on institutional competence. In my twenties I probably cared more about which side sounded right to me culturally. Now I ask whether a policy can actually be implemented, who it helps, and what the second-order effects are. The pandemic also changed me because it showed how fragile trust is when public communication is bad. The 2020 racial justice protests pushed me to take policing and racial disparities more seriously instead of treating them as distant issues. I am still center-left, but I am more concrete and less slogan-driven than I used to be.

follow_ups.question: Was there a specific event that made competence more important to you?
follow_ups.response: The pandemic response, absolutely. Watching institutions communicate poorly made me realize good intentions are not enough.

follow_ups.question: Have your family conversations changed too?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I ask more questions now and argue a little less, though I do not always succeed.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me a lot, especially in 2020 and after. I would not pretend I was completely unaware before, but seeing the protests, listening to Black coworkers and friends, and hearing how different their experiences with police or public spaces were made it more personal. It also made me look back at situations where I had assumed my experience was normal when really it was protected by being white and middle-class. I did not suddenly become an expert, but I became less comfortable being passive. At work, it changed how I think about hiring, mentorship, and who gets the benefit of the doubt.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone close to you influence how you thought about it?
follow_ups.response: Marcus did. He shared a couple of stories about traffic stops that sounded nothing like mine, and because I know him well, I could not file it away as abstract.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect your workplace behavior?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I am more intentional about structured hiring criteria and making sure quieter people are not overlooked in meetings.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about them as questions of accountability, dignity, and unequal risk. The phrase itself gets politicized, but the underlying issues are concrete: who gets stopped, who gets believed, who is treated as threatening, who has to manage their tone to stay safe. I do not think every solution is simple, and I know communities also want safety from violence. But I think we can want safety and still demand transparency, better training, alternatives for mental health calls, and consequences for misconduct. I also think white people like me have to resist the urge to only engage when something is in the news.

follow_ups.question: What reforms make the most sense to you?
follow_ups.response: Better data on stops and use of force, independent review, mental health crisis teams, and changing incentives so departments are not rewarded just for arrests or volume.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss these issues at work?
follow_ups.response: Carefully, but yes when it touches hiring, team culture, or current events that are clearly affecting people.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I have been thinking about race less as an individual attitude and more as something built into systems and everyday defaults. I grew up in a mostly white Midwestern environment where being polite was treated almost like proof that everything was fine. As I have gotten older, that feels inadequate. I think about housing, schools, wealth, policing, and workplace networks because those are the mechanisms where history becomes current reality. At the same time, I try not to turn every conversation into me performing guilt. The more useful question is what I actually do differently.

follow_ups.question: What do you do differently now?
follow_ups.response: I read more carefully, I listen longer, and at work I push for clearer promotion criteria so decisions are less dependent on who reminds leaders of themselves.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel comfortable talking about race?
follow_ups.response: More than I used to, but not fully comfortable. I think some discomfort is probably appropriate.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with friends and family, attended one peaceful march in Columbus in 2020, donated small amounts to a local bail and legal support fund, and tried to make workplace decisions more structured. I am not constantly posting about it online.

follow_ups.question: Why not post much online?
follow_ups.response: I do not think my Instagram caption is the main contribution. I would rather talk directly or change something I control.

follow_ups.question: How did your family respond when you talked about it?
follow_ups.response: Mixed. Some were receptive, some got defensive, and a few conversations ended with everyone needing a break.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My friends are mostly aligned with me, though not identical. Marcus is more direct and personally affected, so he has less patience for abstract debates. Priya is very policy-oriented and sends articles or local meeting notes. My parents are sympathetic but sometimes uncomfortable with the language around privilege or systemic racism. My dad especially can get stuck on the idea that his family worked hard too, and I try to say that both things can be true. At work, people vary, and I have learned not to assume silence means agreement or disagreement.

follow_ups.question: Who do you learn from most in those conversations?
follow_ups.response: Probably Marcus and Priya, in different ways. Marcus grounds it in lived experience, and Priya pushes me toward policy details.

follow_ups.question: Have any relationships been strained by politics?
follow_ups.response: A little, mainly with extended family on Facebook. I have muted more than argued because arguing there rarely improves anything.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say I am healthy. I am 36, I play pickup basketball weekly, I hike, and I do body-weight workouts or cardio a few times a week when my schedule cooperates. I do carry stress physically, mostly tight shoulders, stomach tension, and bad sleep when a deal is going sideways. I have some anxiety tendencies, not a dramatic crisis every day, but enough that I take mindfulness and journaling seriously. I drink coffee, probably too much, and I like wine with dinner, so moderation is something I pay attention to. I have health insurance through work and a primary care doctor I see for annual visits.

follow_ups.question: How many days a week do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Usually three or four. Basketball once, two shorter workouts, and a hike or long walk if the weekend allows.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when stress affects your sleep?
follow_ups.response: I try to stop screens earlier, write down the thing I am looping on, and sometimes do a guided meditation. It does not always work, but it helps.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when my calendar has structure because I can plan workouts, meals, and sleep. It is hard during quarter-end or travel weeks because I am eating restaurant food, sitting in calls, and running on adrenaline. Having friends who play basketball and hike makes exercise social, which helps a lot. The hardest part is emotional regulation: if I am stressed, I want salty food, wine, and late-night scrolling. I know the pattern, but knowing it and stopping it are not always the same thing.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit is most reliable for you?
follow_ups.response: Basketball, because other people expect me to show up.

follow_ups.question: What habit slips first?
follow_ups.response: Sleep. If work is intense, I stay up too late trying to get one quiet hour back.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge, thankfully. I sprained my ankle playing basketball last year, and that knocked me out for about six weeks. It was frustrating because exercise is one of my main pressure valves. I also had a stretch of tension headaches during a bad work quarter, and my doctor basically told me what I already knew: hydrate, sleep, reduce stress, and stop treating coffee as a food group. No major diagnoses, no broken bones, no chronic condition that I am managing daily. I did start seeing a therapist monthly for anxiety and stress management, which I consider health care even if it is not a dramatic diagnosis.

follow_ups.question: Did you do physical therapy for the ankle?
follow_ups.response: A few sessions and then exercises at home. I still do calf raises and balance work when I remember.

follow_ups.question: How did you find the therapist?
follow_ups.response: Through my insurance directory and a recommendation from a friend who said therapy was useful even if nothing was on fire.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not seriously stopped me from working. The ankle injury changed my workouts and made me cranky, and anxiety can make a workday harder, but I have not had to leave a job or miss major responsibilities because of health.

follow_ups.question: Have you taken sick days for stress?
follow_ups.response: Once or twice I have taken a day when I was burned out and knew I would be useless. I am getting better at doing that before I snap.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel comfortable telling your manager that?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat. I usually frame it as needing a personal health day, and my workplace is decent about that.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, more with my parents as they get older. Nothing catastrophic right now, but my dad has blood pressure and cholesterol issues, and my mom had knee replacement surgery a couple of years ago. I helped with rides, grocery runs, and figuring out patient portal messages after her surgery. It made me realize that even routine medical stuff becomes a family logistics project. My sister helps too, but because I am single and local, I sometimes have more flexibility to step in. I do worry about what caregiving could look like ten years from now.

follow_ups.question: How do you and your sister divide that help?
follow_ups.response: Gina handles a lot of emotional check-ins and kid-friendly visits, and I handle tech, paperwork, and some transportation.

follow_ups.question: Did your mom recover well from surgery?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she did. The first month was rough, but now she walks better than before.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I am fortunate because I have employer insurance and enough income that I usually do not skip care. The frustrating part is navigating networks, deductibles, and appointment wait times. Therapy was the hardest because a lot of people were not accepting new patients or had weird availability. I have delayed things like dermatology or physical therapy because scheduling felt annoying, but I have not truly had to forgo necessary care because of money. For my parents, Medicare paperwork and portals can be confusing, so I help interpret. The system feels manageable for us only because we have time, education, and someone in the family willing to sit with the forms.

follow_ups.question: Have costs ever surprised you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, physical therapy copays added up faster than I expected. It was not ruinous, but it reminded me how quickly care becomes expensive.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a regular primary care provider?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I see a primary care doctor once a year and message through the portal if something comes up.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing very formal or indigenous. My family definitely has informal remedies: ginger tea, stretching, hot compresses, olive oil for every possible kitchen and life problem, that kind of thing. I have done yoga and meditation, and I have used massage for stress and tight shoulders. My mom is big on herbal teas and broth when someone is sick. I see those as supportive, not replacements for medical care. If something is serious, we go to a doctor.

follow_ups.question: Do you practice yoga regularly?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally. I will do a class or online session when my back or shoulders feel locked up, but it is not weekly.

follow_ups.question: What family remedy do you still actually use?
follow_ups.response: Ginger tea with honey when I feel run down. It may be placebo, but it is comforting.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I do drink, mostly wine or a beer with friends, and I genuinely enjoy pairing wine with food. During stressful periods, I have noticed the urge to pour a glass as a shortcut to relaxing, so I watch that. I am not drinking every night, but quarter-end can make it creep up if I am not careful. Most weeks it is maybe three or four drinks total, sometimes more if there are dinners or events. If I catch myself using it to shut my brain off, I try to take a week mostly off.

follow_ups.question: What kind of wine do you like?
follow_ups.response: Bold reds: Chianti, Barolo if I am splurging, Zinfandel, sometimes a big California cab with steak or mushroom risotto.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever felt drinking was out of control?
follow_ups.response: No, not out of control, but I know enough family and work stress stories to respect how easily a habit can slide.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use prescriptions for anxiety right now, and I do not rely on pain medication beyond ibuprofen after basketball or a headache. I have used marijuana a few times socially, mostly edibles, but it is rare because it can make me feel too inward and anxious. The most recent time was probably at a friend's house last winter; I had a low-dose edible, watched a movie, and mostly decided I would rather have a glass of wine and be clear-headed. I am not morally opposed to it, it just is not my preferred way to cope. My main tools are exercise, therapy, journaling, and trying to sleep.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep marijuana at home?
follow_ups.response: No. If it happens, it is usually because someone else has it in a social setting.

follow_ups.question: Do you take any regular medications?
follow_ups.response: No regular prescriptions. Just vitamins when I remember, which is not as often as the bottle suggests.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I pay through employer-sponsored insurance, payroll deductions, copays, and an HSA. It is manageable for me, though I still get annoyed by the opacity of costs. My parents use Medicare plus supplemental coverage, and my sister has insurance through her job and her husband's job situation. We are not choosing between medicine and rent, which I know is a privilege. The coping part is mostly administrative: tracking appointments, keeping passwords straight, and making sure my parents understand bills before paying them. Health care feels less like one bill and more like a part-time paperwork hobby nobody asked for.

follow_ups.question: Do you contribute financially to your parents' care?
follow_ups.response: Not regularly. I help with time and logistics more than money right now.

follow_ups.question: Do you use your HSA much?
follow_ups.response: Mostly for copays, therapy, and occasional prescriptions. I try to leave some of it invested, but I am not perfect about that.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am pro-vaccination. I got the COVID vaccines and boosters that were recommended for me, and I get a flu shot most years. I see it as a practical public health tool, not a political identity.

follow_ups.question: Was anyone in your family hesitant?
follow_ups.response: A couple of extended relatives were skeptical, but my immediate family got vaccinated.

follow_ups.question: Do you get vaccinated at your doctor's office or pharmacy?
follow_ups.response: Usually a pharmacy because it is convenient.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my primary care doctor first, then sources like the CDC, major hospital systems, and public health experts who explain uncertainty clearly. I also pay attention to what Ohio State's medical system puts out because it feels local and credible. I do not get vaccine information from random social media posts. If something sounds dramatic, I usually look for the original source or a reputable medical explanation. I am comfortable with science changing as evidence changes; what bothers me is people presenting certainty when they are guessing.

follow_ups.question: Do you read medical studies directly?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes abstracts or summaries, but I am not trained to evaluate every detail. I rely on credible interpretation.

follow_ups.question: Do friends ask you about vaccine information?
follow_ups.response: Not much now, but during COVID a few family members would send links and ask if they were legitimate.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: The past year has been productive but emotionally intense. Work has gone well on paper, but managing a sales team means absorbing a lot of pressure from above and anxiety from reps below. I have felt proud, restless, tired, and occasionally lonely. Being single at 36 is mostly fine, but there are weekends when everyone seems to be doing family things and I feel like I missed a turn somewhere. At the same time, I have built a life I genuinely like: friends, basketball, art, cooking, family, and enough money to breathe. My emotional baseline is better when I keep my routines, but when I abandon sleep and exercise, I get sharp-edged fast.

follow_ups.question: When do you feel most lonely?
follow_ups.response: Usually Sunday evenings, especially after a busy weekend when the apartment gets quiet and I start thinking too much.

follow_ups.question: What makes you feel most grounded?
follow_ups.response: Cooking slowly, playing basketball, and having a conversation where nobody is trying to perform.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last fall we lost a major deal that had been in the pipeline for months. I had built the forecast around it, my rep had worked incredibly hard, and when the client delayed indefinitely, I took it personally even though I knew better. I went home, opened my laptop again, and started rewriting strategy notes at 10:30 at night like that would undo the loss. The next day I was short with a coworker, and Leah called me on it in a kind but direct way. That was a rough moment because I realized my stress was leaking onto people. I took a long walk, apologized, and brought it to therapy that week.

follow_ups.question: What did Leah say to you?
follow_ups.response: She basically said, 'You are acting like the whole team failed you, and that is not fair.' It stung because she was right.

follow_ups.question: What did you change after that?
follow_ups.response: I started doing a quick debrief after losses before making any new demands. I try to separate learning from punishment.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: Anxiety is the main one for me. I have not been diagnosed with major depression, and I do not want to overstate it, but I can get anxious, reactive, and mentally stuck on worst-case scenarios. It shows up as over-preparing, checking metrics too often, or replaying conversations. Therapy has helped me see the pattern before it becomes my whole personality for the day. Meditation helps too, though I am not some perfectly serene person. I am more like someone who needs tools because the engine runs hot.

follow_ups.question: Have you received a formal anxiety diagnosis?
follow_ups.response: My therapist has described it as generalized anxiety tendencies, but I am not on medication and I have not treated it as a big clinical identity.

follow_ups.question: Who notices it first when you are anxious?
follow_ups.response: Probably Leah at work or my sister. They can hear when I start talking faster and trying to control every variable.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: My family is doing okay, but everyone carries stress differently. My parents worry about health and retirement stuff, my sister balances work and parenting, and I try to be supportive without turning into the family project manager.

follow_ups.question: Does your family talk openly about mental health?
follow_ups.response: More than we used to. My generation is more comfortable naming anxiety, while my parents still sometimes call it 'being wound up.'

follow_ups.question: Do they know you go to therapy?
follow_ups.response: Yes, my immediate family knows. My mom is supportive, and my dad is supportive in a quiet, slightly confused way.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I was raised Catholic, and culturally that is still part of me. We went to Mass more when I was a kid, especially around holidays, first communions, weddings, funerals, all of that. As an adult, I do not attend church regularly, and I would describe myself as culturally Catholic and spiritually open rather than devout. I still like the rituals, the candles, the music, and the way church can mark time and grief. I struggle with parts of the institution, especially around sexuality, gender, and abuse scandals. For me, spirituality now is more likely to show up in quiet moments: hiking, art, music, cooking for people, or trying to be less selfish. I still go to Mass with my family on Christmas or Easter sometimes because it matters to my mom.

follow_ups.question: Do you identify as Catholic if someone asks your religion?
follow_ups.response: I usually say Catholic, but not practicing. If the form has 'none' and 'Catholic,' I still tend to choose Catholic because it is part of my background.

follow_ups.question: Do you pray?
follow_ups.response: Not in a formal daily way. I have moments where I ask for patience or strength, but it is more inward than structured.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I use social media, but each platform has a different role. Instagram is the one I enjoy most because I follow artists, galleries, restaurants, travel photographers, and friends. LinkedIn is basically part of work; I post occasionally about sales leadership or tech trends and use it to keep up with clients and peers. Facebook is mostly family and event reminders, and I do not post there much. I use Reddit sometimes for hobby rabbit holes, like hiking gear, Arduino projects, or Cavs discussions. I try to avoid doom-scrolling politics because it spikes my stress and rarely makes me smarter.

follow_ups.question: What do you post on Instagram?
follow_ups.response: Food I cooked, museum shots, hiking views, occasional travel photos, and sometimes a Cavs or Buckeyes story.

follow_ups.question: How much time do you spend on social media in a day?
follow_ups.response: Maybe 45 minutes on a good day, more if I am procrastinating or stressed.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: I do not use social media for financial support, and I rarely use it for emotional support. If I am struggling, I text a friend, call my sister, talk to my therapist, or go play basketball.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever posted publicly about a hard time?
follow_ups.response: Not really. I might make a vague reflective post, but I do not process the raw stuff publicly.

follow_ups.question: Who would you text first?
follow_ups.response: Depending on the issue, either Marcus, Leah, or my sister Gina.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: My stress has been a little lower since I changed my morning routine and got more serious about therapy. Work is still intense, but I am better at catching the spiral earlier instead of pretending I can outwork it.

follow_ups.question: What coping strategy works fastest?
follow_ups.response: A walk without headphones. It sounds simple, but movement and quiet help me sort the noise.

follow_ups.question: What coping strategy are you trying to reduce?
follow_ups.response: Late-night scrolling and stress-snacking. Those feel good for ten minutes and then make everything worse.

follow_ups.response: Yes, utilities are in my name.

transcript.response: The biggest expense was rent, about $1,450. After that it was student loan payment, car payment and insurance, groceries and dining out, utilities, and a couple of discretionary things like a framed print and new hiking shoes.

transcript.response: Last month was around $5,600 total, which is a little higher than usual because of the hiking shoes, the print, and a couple of dinners out. A normal month is more like $4,700 to $5,000 including rent, bills, debt payments, groceries, gas, and some social spending.

follow_ups.question: Do you track that in a budget app?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I use a budgeting app and a spreadsheet for bigger goals. Very on-brand for me.

follow_ups.question: What category surprises you most?
follow_ups.response: Dining out and coffee. It never feels like much in the moment, and then the monthly total looks judgmental.

transcript.response: I rent my apartment. I have thought about buying in Columbus, but prices and interest rates have made me cautious, and I do not want to buy just because I feel like I am supposed to.

follow_ups.question: Are you actively looking to buy?
follow_ups.response: Not actively. I browse listings and run numbers, but I am not making offers.

follow_ups.question: What would you want in a home?
follow_ups.response: A small house or condo with a decent kitchen, a home office, and access to walkable places.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Utilities go up in winter because of heat and in summer because of AC. The holidays are expensive because gifts, family meals, and travel all hit at once. Summer can get pricey with weddings, weekend trips, and outdoor gear. My spending also spikes around quarter-end sometimes because I am tired and buy convenience: takeout, rideshares, coffee, whatever keeps the machine moving.

follow_ups.question: What is your most expensive season?
follow_ups.response: Probably December, followed by summer if there are weddings or trips.

follow_ups.question: Do work commissions fluctuate too?
follow_ups.response: Yes. My base salary is steady, but commission or bonus income can vary by quarter.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: I covered them from regular checking and a short-term savings buffer. If I overspend in one month, I usually tighten restaurants, shopping, and travel the next month rather than carrying credit card debt.

follow_ups.question: What do you cut first?
follow_ups.response: Restaurants, art purchases, and random Amazon buys.

follow_ups.question: Do you use credit cards?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for points and tracking, but I pay them off monthly.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: I save in a few ways. I have an emergency fund in a high-yield savings account, I contribute to my 401k, and I put some money into a brokerage account when commissions are good. I automate part of it because if I wait to see what is left, lifestyle creep eats it. I am not perfect; I still impulse-buy food, travel, or art sometimes. But compared with my twenties, I am much more disciplined. The goal is to have choices, not just a bigger number on a screen.

follow_ups.question: How many months of expenses are in your emergency fund?
follow_ups.response: About four months if I am honest, depending on what I count as necessary spending.

follow_ups.question: What motivates you to save?
follow_ups.response: Freedom. I want to be able to take a career risk someday without panicking after one bad month.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: In the last year I have saved for three things: emergency cushion, eventual home down payment, and travel. The home fund is real but not aggressive enough to buy immediately. I also have a mental fund for a Pacific Coast Highway road trip because I want to do that without putting it on a credit card. Long-term, I am saving for flexibility in my career, maybe business school alternatives, executive coaching certifications, or eventually starting a consulting firm. I like experiences, so I have to deliberately protect savings from my own 'life is short, book the trip' impulse.

follow_ups.question: How much do you try to save monthly?
follow_ups.response: Usually $1,200 to $1,800 across cash, retirement, and investments, more if a commission check lands.

follow_ups.question: What is the next big thing you expect to spend on?
follow_ups.response: Probably travel, maybe that Pacific Coast Highway trip, unless I decide to move apartments.

transcript.response: I still have student loans, around $17,000 left, and a car loan around $8,000. I use credit cards but do not carry a balance month to month. I do not owe money to family or friends.

follow_ups.question: Are the student loans federal or private?

follow_ups.question: Are you paying extra on either loan?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes on the car loan when cash flow is good, but I balance that against saving and investing.

transcript.response: I have not been in a situation this past year where I could not pay a necessary bill or buy something I needed. I have delayed wants, like travel or a nicer piece of art, but not necessities. I know that is a privileged position. The closest thing was a month with a dental bill, car repair, and holiday costs all together, and I had to pull from savings temporarily. It was annoying but not a crisis.

follow_ups.question: How did you rebuild the savings after that?
follow_ups.response: I cut dining out for a month and used part of a commission payment to refill it.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever help family financially?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally small things, like picking up dinner or buying something for my nephew, but not regular support.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: I am a sales manager in B2B technology. The simplest version is that I manage a team of account executives and help them move complex deals from first conversation to signed contract. Day to day, I review pipeline, coach reps, analyze conversion rates, join client presentations, work with marketing and product, and forecast revenue for leadership. A big part of the job is translating messy human conversations into data without forgetting that there are humans behind the data. I am very hands-on with Salesforce because if the CRM is sloppy, the forecast is fiction. I also spend a lot of time helping reps tell a clearer story, especially when the product is technical and the buyer is overwhelmed. The most important duties are coaching, prioritizing, negotiating, and keeping the team emotionally steady when the quarter gets intense.

follow_ups.question: What makes you good at that work?
follow_ups.response: Pattern recognition and communication. I can look at a deal and see where the story is weak, then help the rep make it clearer.

follow_ups.question: What is the hardest part?
follow_ups.response: Managing pressure without passing it down in a toxic way. Sales urgency can become panic if you are not careful.

His response to Black Lives Matter includes listening to Black friends and coworkers, attending one peaceful march, making small donations, and applying structured fairness principles at work (Q26, Q27, Q29). He has moderate-to-high civic engagement through voting, local issue attention, and community networks, but he is not a high-intensity activist (Q23, Q29, Q30).
summaries.psychologist: John presents as conscientious, analytical, socially attuned, ambitious, and emotionally reactive, with a strong need to convert uncertainty into plans, metrics, and routines (Q15, Q18, Q45, Q65). He experiences anxiety tendencies marked by over-preparation, rumination, and physical stress, but actively uses therapy, meditation, journaling, exercise, and walks to regulate himself (Q31, Q33, Q43, Q45, Q50). His self-concept blends Midwestern practicality, Italian-American family warmth, technical competence, creative curiosity, and a desire to lead without burning people out (Q01, Q47, Q65, Q108). Relationally, he is close to family and friends but sometimes struggles to slow down enough for connection, especially when work pressure activates his controlling side (Q05, Q07, Q44, Q109).
